background.definition: Food poisonings comprise various acute syndromes resulting from ingestion of contaminated foods. Most, but not all, food poisonings have a component of diarrhea. Manifestations range from slight discomfort to acute illness to severe reactions that rarely may lead to death or chronic sequelae. This chapter excludes accidental/intentional ingestions with chemicals, poisons, overdosages, and other toxins (including mushrooms and heavy metals).

list.listitem: Highest incidence in developing countries: annual Shigella incidence per 100,000 is 318 in India, 219 in East Africa, 120 in West Africa, and 76 in North Africa; the US annual incidence is 6.1 per 100,000.

Estimated incidence (for the year 2015) per 100,000 in the United States is 14.8 for Salmonella, 12.7 for Campylobacter, 6.1 for Shigella, 1.3 for E. coli O157, 0.5 for E. coli non-O157, 0.4 for Yersinia, 0.3 for Vibrio, and 0.1 for Listeria (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [CDC]. Surveillance for Foodborne Disease Outbreaks, United States, 2015, Annual Report, Atlanta, Georgia: US Department of Health and Human Services, 2017).

In 2015 (most recent year reported), data were reported on 902 outbreaks in the US, which resulted in 15,202 cases of foodborne illness, 950 hospitalizations and 15 deaths. Among the 443 outbreaks with a confirmed single etiologic agent, most were caused by bacteria (52%) and viruses (40%). Chemical agents caused 7% and parasites 1%. Norovirus was the most common cause of single agent illness (37%) followed by Salmonella (34%). Among the deaths, 14 were attributed to bacterial etiologies (9 Salmonella, 2 Clostridium botulinum, 1 Clostridium perfringens, 1 Listeria monocytogenes, 1 Vibrio vulnifcus, and1 to viral etiologies (Norovirus).
The Global Burden of Disease Study estimated that there were 535,000 cases of non-typhoidal invasive salmonella disease in 2017, with the greatest incidence in sub-Saharan Africa.
WHO guidelines estimate that there are 165 million diarrheal episodes caused by Shigella annually, with 99% occurring in developing countries.
In the developing world most of the mortality is in children; in the United States, mortality is highest in the elderly population.
In the United States an estimated $6 billion is spent each year on medical care and lost productivity due to foodborne diseases.
Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella, Clostridium perfringens
E. Coli O157:H7, E. coli non-O157
Norovirus
Yersinia, Vibrio, Listeria, Bacillus, botulism
Toxoplasma gondii, Listeria monocytogenes
Various causes of fish and shellfish poisoning (eg, algal toxins, biotoxins)
Virtually any food can become contaminated through inadequate temperature control, infected food handlers, contaminated raw ingredients, cross-contamination, or inadequate heat treatment.
Effects depend on the nature of the agent, the dose (number of microorganisms or concentration of toxins ingested), and the host susceptibility and reaction. Three mechanisms are listed below.
Toxin-mediated infections caused by enterotoxins made during bacterial colonization and growth in the intestinal tract.
Direct bacterial invasion and multiplication in the intestinal tract.
Intoxication caused by poisonous chemicals or toxins produced by microorganisms before ingestion.

The average incubation period for invasive listeriosis is 8 days (range 1-67 days), however the average was different by clinical form of the disease (in pregnancy was 27.5 days, CNS disease 9 days, and bacteremic disease 2 days).

There is now an oral cholera vaccine approved by the FDA that is safe and effective for those traveling to an endemic area. Its efficacy is not establish in persons already dwelling in endemic countries.
Salmonella typhoid vaccine is available for persons planning to live in endemic areas, B but not recommended for most tourists.
Regarding food in endemic areas, remember to “boil it, cook it, peel it or forget it.” C See traveler's diarrhea chapter for prevention of traveler's diarrhea.

Pregnant women should be educated regarding the risk of consuming "ready to eat" food products as well as other processed foods such as deli meats, hot dogs and soft cheeses due to the risk of invasive Listeriosis.

A challenge trial randomized 28 adults to rifaximin 550 mg twice daily or placebo and then innoculated them with campylobacter jejuni; there was no difference in the likelihood of subsequent signs and symptoms (87% vs 85%).

Wilderness Society guidelines note the following temperatures required to kill each pathogen (boiling points will differ by altitude):
Giardia and entamoeba histolytica: 50 C for 10 minutes, 55 C for 5 minutes, or 100 C immediately Cryptosporidium oocysts: 55 C for 20 minutes or 64 C within 2 minutes Common bacterial pathogens (e.g. E. coli, Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella: 55C for 30 minutes or 65 C for .ess than 1 minute Viruses: 56 to 60 C in less than 20 to 40 minutes HepatitisA: 98C for 1 minute Parasitic egs, larvae and cercariae: 50 to 55 C (no time given)
Ultraviolet radiation and lamp systems are effective. An improvisational technique is to use clear plastic bottles left on a dark surface in sunlight for at least 4 hours.

Chlorine is highly effective and kills or inactivates most bacterial and viral pathogens within 60 minutes. The exceptions are giardia lamblia cysts (90 minutes) and cryptosporidium (500 to 755 minutes).

Filtration systems can also be effective. Biosand filters are described as "a reasonable improved technique for filtration". The size of organisms in micrometers is shown for selected pathogens below; filters should be smaller:
Viruses: 0.03 micrometers E. Coli: 0.5 x 3 to 8 micrometers Campylobacter: 0.2 to 0.4 x 1.5 to 3.5 um Cholera: 0.5 x 1.5 to 3.0 um Giardia cysts (entamoeba histolytica is slightly larger): 6 to 10 x 8 to 15 um Cryptosporidium oocyst: 2 to 6 um
An mRNA vaccine is under development against norovirus.
Most food poisoning is self-limited and does not require any diagnostic testing. C

Use stool cultures to identify specific pathogens in patients with prolonged or bloody diarrhea, severe dehydration, or systemic illness, to guide therapy and improve the detection of outbreaks, which will help guide public health measures.C
Consult with local laboratory/specialists regarding which tests are needed based on clinical suspicion. C
See algorithm in and and for typical presentation of different foodborne illnesses.

History should address whether vomiting or diarrhea are primary symptom; type of diarrhea (bloody vs nonbloody), presence and severity of abdominal pain; duration of symptoms; and any systemic symptoms.
In a follow-up study of a food-related outbreak of Salmonella hadar, musculoskeletal symptoms were common (65%), including reactive arthritis (10%).
Ask about neurologic symptoms (botulism, fish and shellfish poisoning, mushroom poisoning).
Obtain travel history, history of high-risk food ingestion (raw or undercooked foods; unpasteurized dairy or juices; home-canned foods; seafood; soft cheeses).
Assess hydration.

Frankly bloody diarrhea is diagnostic for invasive pathogens. In patients with nonbloody diarrhea, the findings that best rule in invasive diarrhea when present are tenesmus and moderate or heavy mucus.
Most food poisoning is self-limited and does not require any diagnostic testing.

In patients with bloody stools, severe abdominal pain, or prolonged or severe illness, or in those who are immunocompromised, stool culture is the gold standard (accuracy and value varies). Be aware that certain suspected infections (Vibrio, Yersinia, E. coli O157:H7, and Campylobacter) require specific growth media that need to be specified when ordering cultures.
CDC recommends that patients with acute community-acquired diarrhea be tested for shiga toxin e. coli (STEC) O157.

A systematic review of 34 studies with 28,105 patients found that PCR for campylobacter was highly accurate: 95% sensitive, 97% specific, LR+ 31, LR- 0.05. The test was somewhat less sensitive (87%) in children.
It may be helpful to discuss diagnostic strategies with your local laboratory/health department/specialist prior to testing.

Fecal leukocytes or erythrocytes (or the combination) or lactoferrin increase the likelihood of invasive diarrheal illness and can guide the decision to consider further workup. See and for specific tests.
Antigen and molecular testing can expedite diagnosis (accuracy and value vary).
In the setting of significant systemic illness, blood cultures may be helpful.
Laboratory testing for botulism in the United States is available only at the CDC which has a 24 hour botulism consulting service. EMG can be supportive in diagnosis.
See algorithm in for differential diagnosis.
See for typical presentation of different illnesses and for treatment recommendations.
ORT is best for dehydration; A use other supportive measures. C
Antibiotics are not usually indicated and may worsen outcomes.A
Antidiarrheals are not usually indicated and may worsen outcomes, especially in children. A

Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) for dehydration A and other supportive measures are the first line of treatment. Antidiarrheals are usually not needed, should be avoided in persons with bloody or febrile diarrhea, and should not be used for more than 2 days in any case. C

Antibiotics are usually not indicated and may worsen outcomes by causing hemolytic uremc syndrome. They should be considered for patients with severe salmonella or sepsis (especially if immunocompromised, infants and the elderly) although evidence is poor. B
In cases of suspected botulism, immediately contact the appropriate specialist. C
Standard antidiarrheal agents are not recommended as they have potentially serious adverse affects in young children and infants.
Antibiotics are usually not indicated and may worsen outcomes. Use with known susceptibility (due to rising resistance) and only in severe disease.

For patients with salmonella, CDC guidelines recommend that antibiotics should only be considered for patients with severe illness including sepsis or at risk for severe illness, such as infants, the elderly and persons with immunocompromise. If indicated a fluoroquinolone is recommended for adults and azithromycin for children.

CDC guidance does not recommend antibiotics for suspected shiga toxin producing e. coli (STEC) until diagnostic testing can be completed and STEC is ruled out. The concern is increased risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome with antibiotics.
WHO guidelines recommend either ciprofloxacin, pivmecillinam or ceftriaxone for shigellosis (dysentery) in developing countries.
A 5-7 day course of metronidazole or single-dose treatment with tinidazole is recommended for giardiasis.,
Botulism requires an antitoxin.
A small RCT (n = 24) found no benefit to azithromycin over placebo for campylobacter concisus.
Supportive care is indicated in all patients with foodborne illnesses.
ORT is painless, safe, inexpensive, and superior to IV therapy in individuals who can take oral fluids.
IV therapy may be necessary in the setting of severe dehydration.
A protein-rich diet in malnourished children in endemic areas improves growth and decreases diarrheal morbidity following shigellosis.
Botulism treatment requires supportive care and may require mechanical ventilation.
Hospitalization and referral may be necessary for severe disease (severe dehydration, neurologic involvement, systemic disease).
If the patient is hospitalized, consider a consult with an infectious disease specialist.
Observe closely persons potentially exposed to botulism; for those with signs of botulism, give prompt treatment with antitoxin and supportive care that may include assisted ventilation.

For suspected botulism, immediately contact (1) the hospital epidemiologist or infection control practitioner; and (2) local and state health departments. If the local and state health departments are unavailable, contact the CDC: (404) 639-2206; (404) 639-2888 [after hours]. The CDC can also arrange for shipment of the antitoxin.
Reportable causes of foodborne illness include salmonellosis, shigellosis, and campylobacter. For the complete list see the CDC National Notifiable Disease list.
In the United States most food poisoning is self-limited. C
Younger children, infants, elderly, and other immunocompromised individuals are at an increased risk of morbidity and mortality. B
Children younger than 5 years are at an increased risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). B
Following an episode of acute gastroenteritis, especially with Campylobacter or Proteobacteria, there is an increased likelihood of post-infection irritable bowel syndrome.
The elderly are at an increased risk of morbidity and mortality, usually secondary to dehydration.
Children, especially infants and children younger than 5 years, are at increased risk of morbidity and mortality due to severe dehydration.
The risk of HUS is increased following Salmonella infection, especially for children younger than 5 years.
Infant botulism can be treated with intravenous botulism immunoglobulin (BIG-IV) which helps decrease morbidity associated with the illness.

cell.label: Patient presents with GI symptoms and suspected food-related illness
Consider: – Viral gastroenteritis (eg, rotavirus, norovirus) – Preformed toxins (eg, vomitoxin, Staph aureus toxin, Bacillus cereus toxin) – Heavy metals

Consider any enteric pathogen but is classically symptom of: – Enterotoxigenic E. coli – Vibrio cholerae – Enteric viruses (astroviruses, noroviruses, and other caliciviruses, enteric adenovirus, rotavirus) – Parasites (Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora)
Consider: – Shigella, Campylobacter, Salmonella species – Enteroinvasive E. coli, E. coli O157:H7 – Vibrio parahemolyticus – Yersinia enterocolitica – Parasitic: Entamoeba histolytica

Consider: – Botulism – Scombroid, ciguatera, or tetrodon fish poisoning – Neurotoxic, paralytic, or amnestic shellfish poisoning – Mushroom poisoning – Guillan-Barré syndrome (associated with Campylobacter)
Consider: – Listeria monocytogenes – Brucella species – Vibrio vulnificus – Salmonella typhi and paratyphi
